To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the ancestral butterfly compound eye had nine photoreceptor types that expressed one UV-, one UV–B-, one B–B-, and one LW-absorbing opsins; the UV-, UV–B-, and B–B-absorption visual pigments were expressed in the R1 and R1 photoreceptor cells, and the LW-absorbing opsin was expressed in R3–9 photoreceptors; the ancestral butterfly eye was composed of a main retina and a secondary retina,
the eyes of butterflies are remarkably complex, and that the molecular basis of this complexity is due to the presence of multiple opsin genes that are spatially expressed within each compound eye.

the eyes of butterflies are nearly as diverse and colorful as the wings and that much of this diversity is the consequence of alterations in the number of opsins and the spatial distribution of opsins within eyes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the evolution of visual systems in insects and the role of opsin genes in this process.
understanding how butterfly eyes have evolved.
the molecular mechanisms that control the development of the butterfly eye, and with the molecular basis of the remarkable visual diversity of butterflies.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the butterfly eye is a mosaic of opsins that is the result of an adaptive evolutionary expansion of a relatively simple visual system.
the ancestral butterfly eye contained UV-, B- and LW-absorbing opsins that were expressed in the R1–9 photoreceptors.
the butterfly eye has undergone a remarkable diversification of opsins, which has led to the development of a visual system that is nearly as diverse as their wings.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the butterfly eye has been reconstructed from a single opsin to a complex visual system that is capable of detecting the entire visible light spectrum.
the butterfly eye is an excellent system for the study of eye development and evolution.
the ancestral butterfly eye was composed of a main retina with UV, B and L opsins and a secondary retina with UV and LW opsins.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the ancestral butterfly eye was not as simple as previously thought and that it is possible to reconstruct the eye from the opsin gene expression pattern.
butterfly opsins have undergone a lineage-specific expansion, and that this expansion has resulted in the evolution of new visual capabilities.

the ancestral butterfly eye had a UV–LW opsin gene repertoire, and that this gene set has been expanded in different butterfly lineages by lineage-specific gene duplications and by alterations in gene expression.
